ut_lower_hillside.blurb: Lower Hillside is a small sandstone bouldering zone in the Right Fork of Joe's Valley, reached by driving a few miles up the fork to a pullout beside the road. It holds 13 problems with a wide spread: a handful of easy lines around V0 to V2, a solid middle band through V3 to V6, and a couple of very hard V9 testpieces at the top end. The stone is variable but mostly good, and many of the boulders face south, so they pick up plenty of sun. Sandstone here is much weaker after rain, so give it a couple of dry days before pulling on holds.

ut_nessi_s.blurb: Nessi's is a compact bouldering spot in the Utah West Desert, on the Lake Mountains side near Eagle Mountain, at roughly 4,850 feet. A short dirt-road drive ends at a turnaround, and the line of boulders sits only a few minutes' walk beyond it. There are 13 problems, running from V0 warm-ups through the middle grades up to a V9 at the top end, with several lines packed onto one main boulder. The setting is open and fully exposed with no trees, so expect sun for most of the day and carry your own water.

ut_drilled_pocket_boulder.blurb: Drilled Pocket Boulder is a single roadside sandstone block in Zion National Park, a short walk from the car and not far inside the south entrance. The face that looks toward the road is mostly slab with easy lines on its right side, while the south side carries a crack and the line of drilled pockets that gave the boulder its name, and a few more lines lie around the back. Its 13 problems cover everything from very easy up through the V4-5 range, with one much harder V9 line, so it suits a quick session for mixed abilities. Skip it when the rock or ground is damp, since the sandstone is fragile.

ut_1_swoop_wall.blurb: Swoop Wall is the first wall on the east side of Buckskin Gulch in south-central Utah, about a quarter mile on foot from where you park. The limestone is vertical and edgy with the occasional pocket, and still a little sharp. Most of the 13 climbs are bolted sport lines, mainly in the 5.10 range with a few at 5.9 and a handful in the 5.11s, plus one trad crack and a single boulder problem. It is a fairly small wall, best for climbers comfortable on technical, balance-oriented face climbing rather than steep power moves.

ut_barney_s_phinn_east_face.blurb: Barney's Phinn East Face is one of the walls in the Devil's Fins area of Utah's West Desert, at roughly 6,000 feet. It offers 13 routes, nearly all of them bolted sport lines, with one trad route. The grades run from about 5.6 up to 5.11, but the heart of the wall is the 5.10 range, with a few easier lines in the 5.7 to 5.9 range to start on. The routes are described as long, which makes it a good stop for climbers who want more sustained pitches than a typical short crag offers. The face is reached by hiking past a couple of neighbouring crags and around the south end of the fin.
